title: Adaptive SRE-Mass Cache Sizing for Hybrid Linear Attention

raw.stage1:
### Purpose
The contribution's purpose is to eliminate wasted memory from fixed sparse-cache sizes in hybrid linear attention by sizing the cache to actual per-step recall requirements. None of the prior papers explicitly address this specific problem. While many papers focus on KV cache compression or memory efficiency (e.g., [1], [3], [5], [7], [8], [23]), they do not target the issue of wasted memory due to fixed sparse-cache sizes in hybrid linear attention or dynamically sizing the cache based on recall requirements. This purpose appears to be novel.

### Mechanism
The mechanism, SRE-adaptive-mass caching, dynamically adjusts cache size at each update step by retaining tokens until a target fraction of the Self-Recall Error (SRE) mass is captured. Paper [17] introduces "Adaptive Retention," a probabilistic token selection mechanism that learns which representations to keep under a strict global budget, which is conceptually similar to dynamically adjusting retention based on importance. Paper [14] discusses "Structured Token Retention," which dynamically adjusts token retention thresholds based on probabilistic selection frameworks. Both mechanisms involve adaptive retention strategies based on token importance, which is substantively equivalent to the SRE-adaptive-mass caching mechanism.

### Evaluation
The contribution evaluates its method on RULER long-context benchmarks against LoLA's fixed cache size baseline. Paper [16] introduces SCBench, a KV cache-centric benchmark for long-context methods, which evaluates KV cache optimizations in real-world use cases. Paper [8] evaluates KV cache management frameworks tailored for long-text generation. Both papers use evaluation designs centered around KV cache performance on long-context benchmarks, which matches the evaluation design of this contribution. The specific benchmark instance (RULER) is a parameter change, not a new evaluation design.

### Domain
The domain is efficient LLM inference and KV cache compression. Many prior papers ([1], [3], [5], [7], [8], [23], [24]) work in the same general application area of efficient LLM inference and KV cache compression. While the specific sub-problem (eliminating wasted memory from fixed sparse-cache sizes) is narrower, it still falls within the broader domain of efficient LLM inference and KV cache optimization. Therefore, the domain is covered.

The mechanism is SRE-adaptive-mass caching: a training-free method that retains tokens until a target fraction p of total Self-Recall Error (SRE) mass is captured, dynamically adjusting cache size at each update step.

Paper [13] (FlexPrefill) uses a cumulative attention mass threshold to determine which tokens to retain: it dynamically sizes the sparse attention pattern by accumulating attention scores until a target fraction is reached — this is structurally equivalent to "retain until target fraction of mass is captured." Paper [25] also uses adaptive-k selection based on cumulative signal. Paper [14] uses probabilistic selection that dynamically adjusts token retention. Paper [30] uses RC-based token compression with statistical thresholds. FlexPrefill [13] is the closest: "context-aware sparse attention" that adapts the number of retained tokens based on cumulative attention mass — the same primitive of "accumulate signal mass until threshold p is reached."

Paper [9] evaluates on long-context benchmarks including retrieval-intensive tasks for hybrid linear attention models. Paper [16] (SCBench) is a KV cache-centric benchmark for long-context methods. RULER is a standard long-context benchmark used across multiple papers in this space. Papers [9], [16], and others use long-context benchmark evaluation designs with similar metric semantics. ### Purpose
The contribution's purpose is to show that adaptive cache sizing substantially reduces memory overhead with a small accuracy cost. Paper [7] ("Adaptive Online Cache Capacity Optimization via Lightweight Working Set Size Estimation at Scale") discusses adaptive cache capacity optimization to reduce memory overhead, which aligns with the general goal of adaptive cache sizing. The contribution measures cache size and accuracy of SRE-adaptive-mass caching on RULER Variable Tracking tasks versus a fixed-cache baseline. Paper [11] ("ARC: a self-tuning, low overhead replacement cache") uses adaptive replacement cache mechanisms to dynamically balance recency and frequency components, which is conceptually equivalent to adaptive cache sizing. Therefore, the evaluation design is not covered.
